title: Days, dates and when
blurb: Everything about when. Relative words — yesterday, next week — are built from six prefixes, weekdays from one suffix, months from the number plus gatsu; the marked cells are the handful that break their pattern. The one real split is ni: a calendar slot takes it, a relative word never does.

grids.title: dates — read down the ones digit

rules.title: Six prefixes, twelve words
rules.body: Stick the prefixes onto shuu (week) or getsu (month) and both of those columns fall out with no exceptions: senshuu, konshuu, raishuu, saraishuu. Same for sengetsu, kongetsu, raigetsu, saraigetsu.

rules.title: Year only listens to half of them
rules.body: rainen and sarainen behave. The other four are their own words and have to be learnt flat: ototoshi, kyonen, kotoshi, maitoshi (also heard as mainen).

rules.title: Morning and night are just glue
rules.body: day + no + asa/ban, every time: kinou no asa, ashita no ban, asatte no asa. Only kesa (this morning) and konban (tonight) refuse to play. The mai- row drops the no: maiasa, maiban.

rules.title: The exceptions cluster around now
rules.body: kyou, kesa, konban, kotoshi — the words you say most often are the ones that wore down. Two freebies help: oto- means 'before last' on both scales (ototoi, ototoshi), and the future starts with a (ashita +1, asatte +2). mai- is the one prefix that works in every column.

rules.title: Weekdays: one suffix, the planets' names
rules.body: Every weekday is prefix + youbi, and the seven prefixes are the classical planets — moon, fire (Mars), water (Mercury), wood (Jupiter), gold (Venus), earth (Saturn), sun. It is the same week French and English named, so kayoubi lines up with mardi and mokuyoubi with jeudi. Nothing here is irregular. Japanese calendars usually start the week on Sunday.

rules.title: The apostrophe is a real sound
rules.body: kin'youbi and nan'youbi, not kinyoubi: the n stands on its own and the y starts the next syllable — say kin, then youbi. Asking uses the same shape: nan'youbi desu ka — what day is it?

rules.title: Number + gatsu, always
rules.body: The shape never bends: ichigatsu, nigatsu, sangatsu, gogatsu. Only the number bends its reading — shigatsu, shichigatsu, kugatsu. There is no yongatsu, nanagatsu or kyuugatsu.

rules.title: 4, 7 and 9 again — but not the same way
rules.body: The clock trips on the same three numbers, and only two of them agree: shichiji / shichigatsu and kuji / kugatsu match, but the hour is yoji while the month is shigatsu. 4 is the one to watch.

rules.title: Dates: ten words of their own, three survivors
rules.body: tsuitachi, futsuka, mikka, yokka, itsuka, muika, nanoka, youka, kokonoka, tooka are words of their own — and tsuitachi only means the 1st; one day is ichinichi. Above ten it is the number + nichi (juuichinichi, sanjuuichinichi), except juuyokka (14), hatsuka (20) and nijuuyokka (24), which keep the old reading.

rules.title: ni: calendar slots yes, relative words no
rules.body: A date, a month, a weekday or a clock time takes ni: shigatsu ni, hatsuka ni, getsuyoubi ni, kuji ni. Relative words hook on bare: kyou ikimasu, senshuu ikimashita, mainichi benkyou shimasu — senshuu ni is the usual slip, and itsu never takes it either. Parts of the day sit in between: asa ni hon o yomimasu and asa hon o yomimasu are both fine.

title: Reading the clock
blurb: Two suffixes and numbers you already know. Hour then minute, no word for 'past' or 'to' — but three hours lie about their own number, and the minute suffix flips between fun and pun.

cells.en: 9 a.m. — gozen goes first, unlike English

cells.kana: よじよんじゅうごふん

cells.en: five to eight — mae means before

rules.title: Hour then minute, nothing in between
rules.body: sanji juugofun is 3:15. Japanese has no word doing the work of 'past' or 'to' — you say the hour, then the minutes, and stop.

rules.title: Three hours lie about their number
rules.body: 4 is yoji, not yonji. 7 is shichiji, not nanaji. 9 is kuji, not kyuuji. The other nine hours are just the number plus ji, so these three are the whole memorisation cost.

rules.title: pun after a stopped sound
rules.body: 1, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 10 end in an n or a small tsu, and the f hardens to p: ippun, sanpun, yonpun, roppun, happun, juppun. 2, 5, 7 and 9 stay soft: nifun, gofun, nanafun, kyuufun. Same rule for compounds — 15 is juugofun, 30 is sanjuppun.

rules.title: 4, 7 and 9 switch sides
rules.body: The traps invert between the columns: yoji but yonpun, shichiji but nanafun, kuji but kyuufun. If you learn one column and guess the other, these three are where you'll be wrong.

rules.title: han saves you a mouthful
rules.body: sanji han — half past three. Nobody counts out sanji sanjuppun when talking. And gozen / gogo go in front of the hour, not after it: gozen kuji, gogo sanji.

title: Going somewhere
blurb: One shape carries most travel sentences: when + how + where + verb. The slots are easy; the particles are what goes wrong, so this sheet is mostly them.

cells.en: only with a number: kuji ni
the verb always ends the sentence

grids.title: the ones that trip you up

cells.en: every vehicle: basu de, jitensha de, hikouki de, fune de
already a te-form verb, so no de — aruite ikimasu
a state you are in, so it keeps de
e is written he — same trick as konnichiwa
two words — the past sits on deshita

rules.title: The shape
rules.body: when + how + where + verb, and the topic is usually dropped: senshuu, densha de toukyou e ikimashita. watashi wa only goes in when you are switching who the sentence is about.

rules.title: e is spelled he
rules.body: The destination particle is written he and said e — the same trick as konnichiwa. ni does the same job and is the commoner pick: byouin ni ikimasu. e leans on the direction, ni on the arrival.

rules.title: de is the means, to is the company
rules.body: Anything you travel by takes de: densha de, jitensha de, takushii de. A person you go with takes to: tomodachi to ikimashita. hitori de looks like an exception and is not — alone is a state, not a companion.

rules.title: aruite takes nothing
rules.body: aruite ikimasu — I go on foot. It is already a te-form verb, so nothing follows it. aruite de is always wrong.

rules.title: Time words: ni or nothing
rules.body: kyou, ashita, senshuu, raigetsu, mainichi attach bare. Time with a number or a calendar slot takes ni: kuji ni, shichigatsu ni, tanjoubi ni. Weekdays go either way — getsuyoubi ni ikimasu or getsuyoubi, ikimasu.

title: Big numbers and money
blurb: English groups digits in threes and Japanese groups them in fours, so the whole difficulty of big numbers is where you put the break. Once 10,000 is one word — man — a price reads straight off the page.

cells.en: here the ichi comes back, always
the man block is read first
when you are pointing at it

rules.title: Break the digits into fours, not threes
rules.body: The comma English writes every three digits is the wrong cut here. Split 250,000 as 25|0000 and it reads off directly: nijuugo man. Reading it the English way — two hundred and fifty thousand — forces a conversion every single time, and that is the whole reason big numbers feel hard.

rules.title: hyaku and sen drop the ichi, man never does
rules.body: A hundred is hyaku and a thousand is sen, with nothing in front. Ten thousand is always ichiman — never juusen, and never bare man.

rules.title: Three numbers move the sound: 3, 6, 8
rules.body: sanbyaku, roppyaku, happyaku; sanzen, hassen. These are much easier to hear than to work out, so say them out loud rather than deriving them mid-sentence.

rules.title: Big numbers use yon, nana and kyuu
rules.body: yonhyaku, nanasen, kyuuman. The shi, shichi and ku readings belong to the clock and the calendar — yoji, shichigatsu, kugatsu — and stay out of counting.

rules.title: en is a counter like any other
rules.body: The number then en, with no particle between them: gohyaku en, ichiman'en. Ask with ikura desu ka, or kore wa ikura desu ka when you are pointing.

title: i and na adjectives
blurb: Two families, and only one of them conjugates. An i-adjective carries tense and negation in its own ending; a na-adjective never changes shape at all — desu does the work, exactly as it does after a noun.

cells.en: ends in い, and that い is hiragana
doesn't end in い at all
ends in い but takes な — an exception
the い is inside 有名, not an ending

cells.term: Adj − い + くないです
Adj − い + かったです

cells.kana: おおきくなかったです

cells.term: Adj − い + くなかったです

cells.kana: しずかじゃなかったです

cells.term: Adj + じゃなかったです
the only form that keeps いい

rules.title: Check the last kana, then check underneath it
rules.body: An adjective that ends in い written in hiragana is an i-adjective. kirei and yuumei end in the same sound, but there the い is part of the kanji reading — 綺麗, 有名 — so they take na. There are only a handful of those; learn them as exceptions rather than looking for a rule.

rules.title: i-adjectives conjugate, na-adjectives don't
rules.body: The い ending carries tense and negation itself. A na-adjective never changes shape: desu, deshita and ja nai desu do all the work, exactly as they would after a noun. That is the real split between the two families — everything else follows from it.

rules.title: na only appears in front of a noun
rules.body: shizuka desu has no na. shizuka na heya does. The family is named after that one position, which is also the only place you have to remember it.

rules.title: The negative is itself an i-adjective
rules.body: nai ends in い and conjugates like any other i-adjective. That is why ookiku nai becomes ookiku nakatta desu — and why shizuka ja nai becomes shizuka ja nakatta desu. Both families end up running the same negative, which is the reason ja nai desu is worth preferring: learn nai once and every negative in this sheet falls out of it.

rules.title: ii is the exception worth drilling
rules.body: ii desu, but yoku nai desu, yokatta desu, yoku nakatta desu. Every form except the plain present is built from yoi, and ii is common enough that the wrong form is noticeable.

rules.title: Your textbook will say ja arimasen
rules.body: shizuka ja arimasen and shizuka ja arimasen deshita mean exactly the same as the forms above and are what Minna no Nihongo drills, so recognise them. ja nai desu is the everyday spoken version and keeps the negative identical to the i-adjectives, which is one pattern to hold instead of two. de wa arimasen is the same thing again, formal and mostly written — ja is just the contraction of de wa.

title: Likes, skills, having, kara
blurb: Liking, being good at something, understanding it and having it look like four topics, but they are one sentence: the person takes wa, the thing takes ga, and a state word closes it. kara then joins any of them to what follows — the reason first, the result after.

legend.gloss: marks the thing — never wo here

cells.romaji: donna tabemono ga suki desu ka
cells.en: what kind of food do you like?

たばこがきらいですから

cells.en: because I have things to do

cells.kana: あついコーヒーをのみます

rules.title: The thing takes ga, never wo
rules.body: suki, kirai, jouzu, heta, wakarimasu and arimasu describe a state you are in, not something you do to an object, so what you like, understand or have is marked with ga. sushi ga suki desu — never sushi wo suki desu. It is the most common mistake with all six, and the same ga covers every one of them. Real verbs of doing still take wo: tabako wo suimasen, koohii wo nomimasu.

rules.title: wa is the person, ga is the thing
rules.body: watashi wa nihongo ga sukoshi wakarimasu: wa sets who you are talking about, ga marks what they like, understand or have. When the person is obvious, drop the watashi wa entirely — okane ga arimasen is the normal way to say it.

rules.title: donna asks for a kind
rules.body: donna tabemono ga suki desu ka asks what kind, so the answer names a kind: nihon no tabemono, amai mono, ramen. Answering hai to a donna question is the one reply that doesn't work.

rules.title: amari and zenzen need a negative verb
rules.body: takusan, yoku, daitai and sukoshi go with the positive: takusan arimasu, sukoshi wakarimasu. amari and zenzen only ever go with the negative — amari arimasen, zenzen wakarimasen. amari arimasu is not a sentence; the verb has to agree with the adverb, which is why those rows are marked.

rules.title: arimasu is for things
rules.body: kuruma, okane, jikan, youji, yakusoku — anything that isn't alive — takes arimasu. People and animals take imasu instead: kodomo ga imasu, I have a child. Using arimasu for a person is a mistake Japanese speakers notice immediately.

rules.title: youji ga arimasu is how you say no
rules.body: youji means something to do and deliberately says nothing about what. Answering an invitation with youji ga arimasu kara, chotto… declines without a reason anyone can argue with. yakusoku is concrete: an arrangement with another person.

rules.title: kara comes after the reason
rules.body: English can put because at either end; Japanese can't. The reason comes first and kara closes it, then the result: koohii ga suki desu kara, mainichi nomimasu. Keep desu or masu in front of kara when speaking politely — oishii desu kara, youji ga arimasu kara.

rules.title: The whole scale runs on two words
rules.body: suki and kirai carry it, and totemo and amari do the rest: totemo suki desu at the top, totemo kirai desu at the bottom, maamaa desu in the middle. amari only ever pairs with the negative — amari suki ja nai desu.

rules.title: amari suki ja nai desu is how you say no
rules.body: kirai desu is much blunter than 'I don't like it' and lands closer to 'I hate it', so it is rarely said to someone's face about their cooking or their country. The soft refusals are amari suki ja nai desu and maamaa desu. In the other direction kirai ja nai desu is warmer than it looks — it is a quiet way of saying you actually do like something.

rules.title: Don't call yourself jouzu
rules.body: jouzu praises, so it is for other people: nihongo ga jouzu desu ne is what a Japanese speaker says to you after two words. Saying it about yourself sounds like boasting. About yourself, heta desu, or the modest mada mada desu — not yet, not yet.

rules.title: All four are na-adjectives
rules.body: suki, kirai, jouzu and heta conjugate exactly like shizuka: suki ja nai desu, jouzu deshita, heta ja nakatta desu. kirai ends in い but is na, the same trap as kirei. In front of a noun they take na: suki na tabemono, jouzu na hito.

title: Where things are
blurb: One pattern carries all of it: the place, the thing that is there, and a verb chosen by whether that thing is alive. The slots are easy — the particles and the verb choice are what go wrong.

legend.gloss: glues a thing to its position

cells.en: wa only when it's the topic
a plant is alive but doesn't move: arimasu

こうえんにだれがいますか

cells.kana: かぎはどこにありますか
cells.romaji: kagi wa doko ni arimasu ka

rules.title: ni is where it is, de is where it happens
rules.body: Existence takes ni: kouen ni inu ga imasu. de marks where an action goes on: kouen de asobimasu — I play in the park. Same park, different particle, because being somewhere is not doing something.

rules.title: imasu if it moves by itself
rules.body: People and animals take imasu; everything else takes arimasu. A plant is alive and still takes arimasu — the test is moving under its own power, not being alive. A bus takes arimasu, the driver in it takes imasu.

rules.title: what is there takes ga
rules.body: kouen ni inu ga imasu. Never wo — nothing is being done to the dog. wa appears only when the thing is already the topic, and that flips the sentence round: inu wa kouen ni imasu.

rules.title: dare for people, nani for everything else
rules.body: kouen ni dare ga imasu ka asks which person. An animal is nani, not dare, even though it takes imasu: kouen ni nani ga imasu ka. For a thing it is nani with arimasu.

rules.title: mo plus a negative
rules.body: Nobody is dare mo imasen, nothing is nani mo arimasen. mo takes the place of ga, and the verb has to be negative — dare mo imasu is never a sentence. Same deal as amari and zenzen.

rules.title: a position is a noun, glued on with no
rules.body: ue, shita, naka and the rest are nouns, so they join the thing with no: tsukue no ue, hako no naka. The ni comes after the whole phrase: tsukue no ue ni arimasu. Drop the no and it stops being Japanese.

rules.title: aida needs both things
rules.body: aida is between two named things, and they are joined by to: isu to tsukue no aida. One thing alone cannot have an aida — for beside one thing you want tonari or yoko.

rules.title: asking where turns the sentence round
rules.body: inu wa doko ni imasu ka — the thing comes first with wa, the place is what you don't know. The answer keeps that order: inu wa kouen ni imasu. Compare kouen ni inu ga imasu, which answers what is in the park instead.

title: Counting things
blurb: A number on its own counts nothing — it needs a word attached, and which word depends on the shape of the thing. The counter then sits next to the verb, not next to the noun, which is the part that catches everyone.

regular too: いちだい, さんだい, じゅうだい

いっかい, ろっかい, はっかい, じゅっかい

rules.title: the counter stands by the verb
rules.body: ringo wo mittsu tabemashita — the particle stays on the noun and the number goes next to the verb, like an adverb. English puts it in front of the noun and that is the habit to break: ringo mittsu wo is wrong, and nimai no e is not how you say it.

rules.title: the tsu set runs out at ten
rules.body: hitotsu to kokonotsu, then too with no tsu at all, and that is the end of it. From eleven you use juuichi with a proper counter. This set is the fallback for anything whose counter you don't know, and ikutsu is how you ask it.

rules.title: one and two people are irregular
rules.body: hitori and futari, not ichinin and ninin. From three it is regular — sannin, gonin, rokunin — except four, which is yonin and never yonnin. The question is nannin.

rules.title: the shape picks the counter
rules.body: mai for anything flat and thin: paper, stamps, shirts, plates, tickets. dai for machines and vehicles: cars, TVs, bicycles, computers, fridges. nin for people. mai and dai are regular from one to ten, which makes them the easy two — the whole column is the number with the counter stuck on. nin breaks four times: hitori, futari, yonin, and shichinin, which you will also hear as nananin.

rules.title: spans: four of them are regular, days are not
rules.body: Weeks, months and years just take the number — nishuukan, sankagetsu, gonen. Only 1, 6, 8 and 10 change anything, and they change it the same way everywhere: the sound stops. ikkagetsu, rokkagetsu, hakkagetsu, jukkagetsu. Hours are regular except yojikan and kujikan, the same two the clock already breaks, and jikan is itself a span, so nijikan is two hours and nijikankan is nothing. Days are the column to actually learn: ichinichi for one, then the native date words — futsuka, mikka, yokka — which are spans exactly as they stand. Past ten everything follows the same shape as one and two: juuippun, juunifun.

rules.title: how often: span ni count kai
rules.body: ichinichi ni ikkai, isshuukan ni sankai — the span takes ni, the count takes kai. kai stops the sound after 1, 6, 8 and 10: ikkai, rokkai, hakkai, jukkai, the same four as kagetsu and shuukan. Watch sankai, three times, against sangai, the third floor — same kanji 回 and 階 sound alike, and only three voices it.

rules.title: what it takes is marked with ga
rules.body: jikan ga kakarimasu, okane ga kakarimasu — the time or the money takes ga, the same way arimasu does. Ask with dono kurai for either, or ikura when it is only money. kurai means about and follows the amount: nijikan kurai, rokuman en kurai.
